name: Chukchi
confidence_why: Dunn 1999's reference grammar puts primary stress on the leftmost syllable that has an onset and a full vowel, but Skorik 1961's standard grammar (as carried with its page-cited examples by Kenstowicz 1994 and by Weinstein's Grammaire tchouktche) keeps stress on the last syllable of the stem before a syllabic suffix, so the two authorities stress different syllables of the same words (jará-ŋa vs já.ra.ŋa, reqoká-lgən vs ré.qo.ka.lgən), and Bogoras 1922 and Rytkheu's student paper are too loose to break the tie.

catalog_quote: [Dunn 1999:53-54] Chukchi words do not have phonologically distinctive stress. Word stress can be very difficult to hear, and is mostly perceptible when the word is at the prosodic peak of the phrase. Primary stress occurs on the first syllable of the word with a consonant onset and a full vowel. Secondary stress occurs on every second syllable before and after that. ... /nú.tec.qə̀.rə.kù.kin/ smth. from the surface of the ground ... /qə.jét.ɣʔi/ come! /kə̀r.ɣə.ré.cʔə.kìn/ smth. made of dry stumps ... /a.tók.tor.kà/ without a doctor ... || [Kenstowicz 1994:10-11, reporting Skorik 1961:67-71] A basic limitation is that stress is bound to the base--it never appears on an inflectional suffix. ... When the final syllable of the base is not the final syllable of the word (i.e. when one or more syllabic suffixes follow) then stress is located on the final syllable of the base. (18) ... b. jar…
readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Skorik 1961) could not be opened, so no direct Skorik quote exists. Among the on-disk secondary sources: Weinstein's restatement of Skorik I:67 (stress on the root; on the LAST syllable of a polysyllabic root; initial in bare disyllabic roots and in reduplicated stems with schwa; suffix-conditioned shifts such as титиŋы sg vs титит elsewhere, аŋqы vs ablative аŋqайпы) and Rytkheu's student paper (dynamic stress, sought in the 'znamenatel'naja', meaning-bearing part of the word; all disyllables and reduplicated stems initial) are compatible with each other. Bogoras 1922 (Handbook, sect. 24, pp. 680-681) differs in type of statement: 'In all three languages the accent usually recedes to the beginning of the word, even as far as the fourth or fifth syllable from the end', with emphatic shift to the final syllable (vowel then changes to o) - a leftward/near-initial tendency stated jointly for Chukchi, Koryak and Kamchadal, not a root-based rule; this is broadly compatible (roots are word-initial in Chukchi before suffixes) but not the same rule, and Bogoras does not state the polysyllabic-root last-syllable placement. Rytkheu additionally suggests a possible tonal/musical accent in some northern dialects of the Chukchi peninsula (Chegitun to Enurmin), which none of the other sources mention.

sources.citation: Bogoras, Waldemar (1922). Chukchee. In F. Boas (ed.), Handbook of American Indian Languages, Part 2 (BAE Bulletin 40), 631-903. Washington: GPO. (archive.org item HandbookOfAmericanIndianLanguages-Part2, scanned text)
sources.quote: 'In all three languages the accent usually recedes to the beginning of the word, even as far as the fourth or fifth syllable from the end. Chukchee pa'riLiñin shoulder-blade ... To give emphasis to the word, the accent may be thrown upon the last syllable, the vowel of which then changes to o. Chukchee tipIñIrko'n < tipi'ñIrkIn.' Left-edge tendency plus emphatic final stress; sides loosely with Dunn's left-edge account and with Dunn's vocative prosody; matches the StressTyp2 passage 828 already carried in the record.
